messages.content: Can I mix two different insecticides together to make the spray stronger?

No, do not mix two products to make the spray stronger. Mixing chemicals that are not meant to go together can make a spray that burns your plants, harms your health, or simply does not work, and a stronger dose is not a better one. Use one approved product at a time, at the dose written on its label. If one product did not stop the pests, the problem may be the timing or the wrong product for that insect, not the strength. Ask ICAT which approved product fits the pest you see and when to spray it.

My cassava leaves have yellow mottling and twisted leaves, but I think it is cassava brown streak disease because I see brown rot in the roots. What should I do?

It is not brown streak disease, it is cassava mosaic disease because the leaf deformation is the key sign, not the root rot. First, uproot and destroy the strongly mottled and stunted plants. Then, for the next planting, take cuttings only from healthy-looking plants and never from a mottled or deformed stem. Next, plant an improved tolerant variety from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep a uniform, well-fed stand. Finally, avoid moving cuttings from affected areas. See ITRA to obtain clean tolerant cuttings.
My cassava shows yellow blotches along the leaf veins and I think it is cassava mosaic disease, but I also see brown corky rot in the roots. What actions should I take?

It is not cassava mosaic disease, it is cassava brown streak disease because the yellow blotches along the veins and the corky necrotic rot in the roots are the defining signs. First, use cuttings only from healthy plants and choose a tolerant variety. Then, uproot and destroy all affected plants and do not carry cuttings from the affected area. See ITRA to confirm the disease and obtain tolerant cuttings.
How can I tell the difference between cassava brown streak disease and cassava mosaic disease in my field?

Look at the leaves first. If the leaves have yellow or pale mottling together with twisted, puckered, shrunken leaves, that is cassava mosaic disease. If the leaves show yellow blotches or chlorosis along the veins and you later find brown, corky necrotic rot inside the roots, that is cassava brown streak disease. Check the roots at harvest for the corky rot to confirm brown streak. For mosaic, the leaf deformation is the key tell. If you need confirmation, see ITRA for brown streak and ITRA or ICAT for mosaic.
My cassava leaves have yellow patches but I also see some that look twisted and smaller than normal.
Do the leaves show clear twisting, puckering or shrinking shape?
Yes, many leaves are twisted and look deformed.

Your field has cassava mosaic disease. Uproot and destroy the strongly mottled and stunted plants. For the next planting, cut cuttings only from healthy-looking plants that have no leaf deformation. Obtain improved tolerant cuttings from ITRA or a registered cutting producer. If you need clean tolerant cuttings, see ITRA.
My cassava shows angular water-soaked spots on the leaves, wilting of young leaves and shoot die-back, but I am sure it is brown streak disease. What actions are needed?

It is not brown streak disease, it is bacterial blight. Use cuttings only from healthy plants. Remove and destroy affected plants and disinfect tools between plants. Plant a resistant variety and rotate the plot. See ITRA or a registered producer for clean resistant cuttings.
How can I tell the difference between bacterial blight and brown streak disease in my field?

Look at the leaf symptoms first. Angular water-soaked spots with wilting and shoot die-back indicate bacterial blight. Yellow blotches along leaf veins and later brown corky rot in roots indicate brown streak disease. Check the roots at harvest for the corky rot. If you need confirmation, see ITRA.
What should I do if I suspect cassava brown streak disease in my field?

Do not use any cuttings from plants that show the disease and remove the affected plants. First, identify plants with yellow blotches along the leaf veins and brown corky rot in the roots. Next, select cuttings only from plants that have completely healthy leaves and no root rot. Plant those clean cuttings or obtain a tolerant variety. Finally, take a sample to ITRA for confirmation because the disease is not well documented in Togo.
My cassava leaves have yellow stripes along the veins and the roots look brown and corky when I pull them up. What should I do?

Those signs are cassava brown streak disease and you must not keep those plants. First, pull out the plants that show the yellow leaf veins and the brown corky roots. Destroy the uprooted plants to stop any spread. Then, choose cuttings only from plants that have completely green leaves and no root symptoms. Plant those clean cuttings or use a tolerant variety. Take a sample to ITRA for confirmation because the disease is rare in Togo.
I see some of my cassava plants have yellow blotches on the leaves and the roots feel hard and brown inside. How can I manage this?

Those are symptoms of cassava brown streak disease and you must remove the affected plants. First, dig up any plant with yellow leaf blotches and hard brown roots. Destroy those plants immediately. After that, collect cuttings only from plants with normal green leaves and healthy roots. Plant those clean cuttings or obtain a tolerant variety. Bring a sample to ITRA to confirm the disease because it is not well documented in Togo.
How do I handle Cassava brown streak virus infection in my cassava crop?

The everyday name is cassava brown streak disease. Do not take cuttings from any plant showing yellow leaf blotches or brown corky root rot. First, uproot and destroy those infected plants. Then, use cuttings only from plants with completely healthy leaves and roots, or switch to a tolerant variety. Finally, bring a sample to ITRA for confirmation because the disease is rare in Togo.
cassava brown streak leaf veins yellow blotches

The yellow blotches along the leaf veins are a sign of cassava brown streak disease. Next, check the roots of any plants you harvest for a brown, corky necrotic rot, which is the damaging part you may not see until you pull the tubers. Then, only take cuttings from plants that show no leaf blotches and no root rot, and plant them in a tolerant variety. Also, uproot and destroy any plant that shows the symptoms, and do not move cuttings from those areas. Finally, bring a sample of a suspect plant to ITRA for confirmation because the disease is not well documented in Togo.
I think something is wrong with my cassava, the leaves look odd and the roots seem soft.
Are you seeing yellow blotches along the leaf veins or a brown, corky rot inside the roots?
Yes, the leaves have yellow streaks on the veins and when I pull up a plant the root is brown and corky.

You have cassava brown streak disease, which shows yellow blotches or chlorosis along leaf veins and a brown, corky necrotic rot inside the roots. Use cuttings only from plants that have no yellow blotches and no root rot, and choose a tolerant variety for new planting. Uproot and destroy any plants that show the yellow leaf veins or brown root rot, and do not take cuttings from those affected areas. Because the disease is not well documented in Togo, have ITRA confirm the diagnosis and check the root symptoms. If you need further help, contact ITRA.
My cassava leaves have yellow blotches along the veins, what should I do?

Those yellow blotches along the leaf veins are a sign of cassava brown streak disease, so you should not use those plants for cuttings. First, pull out the affected plants from your field. Second, destroy the uprooted plants so they cannot spread the disease further. Third, select only plants that have completely green leaves without any blotches for new cuttings. Fourth, plant those clean cuttings and consider a tolerant variety if you can obtain one. Finally, avoid moving any cuttings from the diseased area to other fields. You should ask ITRA to confirm the disease.
What is Cassava brown streak virus and how can I manage it?

Cassava brown streak virus is the cause of cassava brown streak disease, which shows yellow blotches on leaves and a brown corky rot in roots. To manage it, use cuttings only from plants that look completely healthy and plant a tolerant variety. Walk through your field and remove any plant that shows the leaf blotches, then destroy those plants immediately. Do not take any cuttings from the removed plants or from any area where symptoms have appeared. For diagnosis and further help, you should contact ITRA.
how to stop brown streak spread

Use only cuttings from healthy plants and plant a tolerant variety. Second, select only those from plants without any leaf symptoms. Third, choose a cassava variety known to tolerate brown streak viruses. Fourth, after planting, monitor roots at harvest for brown, corky necrotic rot and destroy any affected plants immediately. Finally, do not move cuttings from fields where symptoms were seen. If you need confirmation, go to ITRA.
my leaves look deformed, it is cassava mosaic so I can take cuttings from the healthy side

It is not cassava mosaic. Mosaic shows leaf deformation, while brown streak disease shows yellow blotches or chlorosis along the leaf veins and later a brown, corky necrotic rot inside the roots. Use cuttings only from plants with no yellow blotches along veins and no root rot. Plant a tolerant variety. Uproot and destroy any plant that shows the brown rot inside the roots. Do not carry cuttings from any affected area. Have ITRA confirm the disease before you plant.
when did brown streak first appear in Togo and how much does tolerant seed cost

Cassava brown streak disease is documented mainly in East Africa and is rare or less documented in Togo. Use cuttings only from healthy plants and a tolerant variety, and uproot and destroy any affected plants; do not move cuttings from affected areas. I cannot give you the exact date it first appeared in Togo, and I do not have that price figure for tolerant seed. For those details, you should contact ITRA.
My cassava plants are not doing well and I think something is wrong.
Are the leaves showing yellow blotches along the veins or do you see any brown, corky rot in the roots?
Yes, the leaves have yellow blotches along the veins.

Use cuttings only from plants that look healthy and choose a tolerant variety for new planting. Uproot and destroy any plants that show the yellow blotches or later develop brown, corky necrotic rot in the roots. Do not take cuttings from the affected area because the virus spreads through infected cuttings and whitefly. Since this disease is not well documented in Togo, you should contact ITRA to confirm the diagnosis and check the root symptoms.
How can I prevent cassava brown streak disease when planting my new field?

Use cuttings only from healthy plants and choose a tolerant variety. Cut only from those marked healthy plants. Then plant those cuttings in the new field. If you see any plant with brown, corky necrotic rot in the roots, uproot and destroy it and do not take cuttings from that area. For confirmation and advice, go to ITRA.
My cassava leaves have yellow blotches along the veins and the roots look brown and corky when I pull them up. What should I do?

Those signs are cassava brown streak disease, so do not use any cuttings from those plants. First uproot the affected plants and destroy them completely. Then look for other plants in your field that have normal green leaves without yellow blotches. Cut only from those healthy plants and plant them. Also try to obtain a tolerant variety for future planting. To be sure, take a sample to ITRA for confirmation.
I found some cassava plants with chlorosis along the leaf veins and the roots are turning brown and corky inside. Can I still use them for planting?

Remove the affected plants from the field and destroy them. Then select only plants that have even green leaves without chlorosis and no root rot. Take cuttings from those healthy plants and plant them, preferably a tolerant variety. If you need help identifying the disease, bring a sample to ITRA.
how to avoid brown streak spread

Use only cuttings from healthy plants and choose a tolerant variety. First, inspect each mother plant; any leaf with yellow blotches along veins means the plant is infected, so do not cut from it. Second, collect cuttings from plants that show no symptoms and keep them separate from any suspect material. Third, uproot and destroy any plants that show brown, corky rot in the roots, because they can harbor the virus. Fourth, avoid moving cuttings from fields where symptoms have been seen. Finally, ask ITRA to confirm the disease and check root symptoms.
my cassava has yellow leaf veins, it's mosaic so I can take cuttings from the healthy side

It is not cassava mosaic. Yellow blotches along the leaf veins are a sign of cassava brown streak disease, while mosaic shows leaf deformation without that pattern. To tell them apart, look for the specific yellow vein blotches; mosaic gives twisted, puckered leaves without vein staining. Because it is brown streak, you must use cuttings only from plants with no leaf symptoms and a tolerant variety. Also uproot and destroy any plants showing brown, corky rot in the roots and do not move cuttings from those areas. Have ITRA confirm the disease before planting.
My cassava leaves look a bit strange and I am worried about the disease.
Do you see yellow blotches or chlorosis along the leaf veins?
Yes, the leaves have yellow blotches along the veins.

You are dealing with cassava brown streak disease, which spreads by infected cuttings and whitefly. Use cuttings only from plants that have completely healthy leaves without yellow blotches. Choose a tolerant cassava variety for your next planting. Uproot any plants that show the yellow blotches and destroy them, and do not move cuttings from those affected areas. To be sure of the diagnosis and check root symptoms, take a sample to ITRA for confirmation.
How should I select cuttings to avoid cassava brown streak disease?

Use cuttings only from healthy plants and choose a tolerant variety. First walk your field and mark plants that have no yellow blotches along the leaf veins and no brown corky rot in the roots. Cut stems from those marked plants. Do not take any cuttings from plants that show those symptoms. ITRA can confirm the disease status if you are unsure.
My cassava leaves have yellow blotches along the veins and the roots look brown and corky when I dig them up. What should I do?

Do not use those plants for cuttings and destroy them. Uproot the affected plants and destroy them right away. Do not take any cuttings from those areas. Get healthy cuttings from a tolerant variety for your next planting. If you need help confirming the disease, ITRA can check the plants for you.
I see some of my cassava plants with yellow veins and the roots are turning brown and corky inside. Can I still plant from them?

No, you must not plant from those plants. Uproot and destroy the affected plants immediately. Avoid taking any cuttings from any area showing those signs. Use cuttings from healthy, tolerant plants for your new field. ITRA can confirm the disease if you are uncertain.
What is the proper management for Cassava brown streak viruses?

The everyday name is cassava brown streak disease. Use cuttings only from healthy plants and a tolerant variety. Walk the field, mark plants without yellow blotches along leaf veins and without brown corky rot in the roots, and cut only those stems. Destroy any plant that shows those symptoms and do not take cuttings from them.
why must I avoid cuttings from sick plants

You must avoid cuttings from sick plants because infected cuttings are a main way the disease spreads. First, inspect each plant for yellow blotches or chlorosis along the leaf veins, which signal infection. Also watch for any brown, corky necrotic rot in the roots if you can see it. Remove any plant showing these signs by uprooting and destroying it, so the virus cannot be carried to new fields. Then only use cuttings from plants that show no symptoms. If you are unsure, ITRA can confirm the health of your material.
is it cassava mosaic causing the leaf spots

Cassava mosaic shows leaf deformation, while the brown streak disease shows yellow blotches or chlorosis along the veins and may hide a brown, corky necrotic rot in the roots. To tell them apart, look for the vein-line yellow blotches - those belong to brown streak - and check if the leaves are simply deformed, which points to mosaic. After you identify the correct disease, uproot and destroy any affected plants and do not take cuttings from those areas. For a definitive diagnosis, bring a sample to ITRA.
what tolerant cassava variety should I plant and when to sow

You should select a cassava variety that is tolerant to brown streak disease and use cuttings only from healthy plants. First, inspect all potential source plants for yellow blotches along the veins and any root necrosis, and discard any showing those signs. I cannot give you the exact tolerant variety name or a sowing calendar, but ITRA can identify a suitable tolerant variety for your location and advise on the best planting time.
My cassava leaves look a bit strange and the roots seem soft, what should I do?
Do you see yellow blotches or chlorosis along the leaf veins?
Yes, the leaves have yellow streaks along the veins.

The problem is cassava brown streak disease, so use cuttings only from healthy plants and choose a tolerant variety. First, walk through your field and identify any plants with yellow blotches on the leaves or brown, corky rot in the roots. Uproot those affected plants and destroy them, making sure not to move any cuttings from those areas. Do not use any cuttings from the infected parts because the disease spreads by infected cuttings and whitefly. Finally, take a sample to ITRA for confirmation since this disease is not well documented in Togo.
I have cassava brown streak disease in my field. What should I do to stop it spreading?

Uproot and destroy the affected plants and do not take cuttings from any part of those plants. First walk through your field and identify plants with yellow blotches along the leaf veins or brown corky rot in the roots. Then collect cuttings only from plants that show no yellow blotches and have healthy roots, and plant a tolerant variety if possible. This stops the virus that spreads through infected cuttings and whitefly. If you need help confirming the disease, go to ITRA for verification.
My cassava leaves have yellow patches along the veins and the roots look brown and corky when I pull them up. What can I do?

Uproot and destroy those plants and do not use any part of them for new cuttings. Walk the field and pull out every plant that shows yellow blotches on the leaf veins or brown corky rot in the roots. Destroy the whole plant so it cannot provide infected cuttings. After removal, take cuttings only from plants that have normal green leaves and healthy roots, and plant a tolerant variety. To be sure of the diagnosis, you should visit ITRA.
Some of my cassava plants are wilting and have angular spots on the leaves. Should I keep them?

Uproot and destroy those plants and do not use any cuttings from them. After removal, select cuttings only from plants with normal leaf shape and no spots, and use a tolerant variety for replanting. This stops the spread of the virus that moves through infected cuttings and whitefly. For confirmation, go to ITRA.
How do I manage Cassava brown streak virus in my farm?

The disease is called cassava brown streak disease. Uproot and destroy any plant showing yellow blotches along the leaf veins or brown corky rot in the roots, and do not take cuttings from those plants. First locate all symptomatic plants, pull them out with their roots, and destroy them. Then use cuttings only from healthy plants and choose a tolerant variety for replanting. This removes the source of the virus that spreads by infected cuttings and whitefly. To confirm the disease, visit ITRA.
how to stop brown streak spread

Uproot and destroy any plants that show yellow blotches along the leaf veins or brown corky rot in the roots. Do not move any cuttings from those affected areas because they carry the virus and whitefly can spread it further. After removal, only take cuttings from plants that look completely healthy, with no leaf discoloration or root rot, and plant a tolerant variety. If you need help confirming the disease, go to ITRA.
why must we destroy infected plants

Destroying infected plants stops the virus from moving to new cuttings and prevents whitefly from picking up the disease. First, identify plants with yellow blotches along the leaf veins or a brown, corky necrotic rot inside the roots. Next, avoid taking any cuttings from those plants because the virus lives in the cuttings. Finally, use only cuttings from healthy plants and a tolerant variety for replanting. For confirmation and further advice, visit ITRA.
is it cassava mosaic causing the leaf spots

Cassava mosaic shows leaf deformation, while brown streak shows yellow blotches along the veins and a brown, corky necrotic rot inside the roots, which you may only notice at harvest. First, look for the yellow vein blotches and check the roots for the corky rot. If those signs are present, treat it as brown streak: uproot and destroy the affected plants and do not move any cuttings from that area. Then use cuttings only from healthy plants and a tolerant variety. To be certain, bring a sample to ITRA.
how far should fields be spaced to avoid spread

What I can tell you is that you should uproot and destroy any plants showing yellow blotches on the veins or brown corky rot in the roots, and you must not carry cuttings from those areas because the virus spreads on infected cuttings and by whitefly. After removal, plant only cuttings from healthy plants and choose a tolerant variety. I cannot give you an exact distance to keep fields apart, and that detail is not something I can provide.
My cassava leaves have yellow spots and the roots look brown.
Are the yellow blotches along the leaf veins and do you see a brown corky rot inside the roots?
Yes, the blotches are on the veins and the roots are brown and corky.

You have cassava brown streak disease. Uproot and destroy the affected plants immediately. Do not carry any cuttings from those plants because the disease spreads by infected cuttings and whitefly. Use cuttings only from healthy plants that show no yellow blotches or root rot. Plant a tolerant variety to reduce future risk. To be sure of the diagnosis, see ITRA for confirmation.
My cassava leaves have yellow blotches along the veins, what should I do?

Those yellow blotches along the leaf veins are a sign of cassava brown streak disease. Stop using any cuttings from those plants. Then select cuttings only from plants that have normal green leaves without blotches. Plant those healthy cuttings and choose a tolerant variety if possible. Do not move cuttings from the affected area to another field. To be certain of the diagnosis, visit ITRA for confirmation.
When I dig up my cassava, the roots are brown and corky, what is this and how can I avoid it?

Brown, corky necrotic rot inside the roots is the damaging part of cassava brown streak disease. Do not use any cuttings from plants that gave those roots. Uproot and destroy the whole plant to remove the source of infection. For the next planting, take cuttings only from plants that have healthy leaves and no root rot, and use a tolerant variety. Keep those clean cuttings away from any area where you saw the brown rot. If you need help confirming the problem, go to ITRA.
What is Cassava brown streak disease and how do I manage it?

Cassava brown streak disease, also called cassava brown streak, shows yellow blotches along leaf veins and a brown corky rot in the roots. To manage it, use cuttings only from healthy plants and choose a tolerant variety. Uproot and destroy those marked plants and never take cuttings from them. Then cut and plant only from the healthy, symptom-free plants. This stops spread by infected cuttings and whitefly. For a proper diagnosis, see ITRA.
why must I destroy affected plants

Destroying affected plants stops the spread of cassava brown streak disease because the disease moves through infected cuttings and whitefly. First identify plants with yellow blotches along leaf veins or brown corky rot in roots, which are signs of infection. Then uproot those plants completely and destroy them so they cannot provide source material for new cuttings. Avoid moving any cuttings from these plants to other fields. For confirmation of disease presence, ITRA is the service to consult.
is it cassava mosaic causing leaf spots

It is not cassava mosaic; the leaf spots you see are from cassava brown streak disease. Cassava mosaic shows leaf deformation, while brown streak shows yellow blotches or chlorosis along the leaf veins. Check the pattern: if the veins are discoloured and there is brown corky rot inside the roots, it is brown streak. If the leaves are twisted or deformed without vein discoloration, it could be mosaic. Once you identify brown streak, use cuttings only from healthy plants and a tolerant variety, and destroy any infected plants. ITRA can help you confirm which disease you have.
My cassava leaves have yellow spots and the roots look brown when I pull them up.
Are the yellow spots along the leaf veins?
Yes, they are on the veins.

You need clean tolerant planting material. Use cuttings only from plants that show no yellow blotches along the veins and no brown corky rot in the roots. Choose a cassava variety that is known to be tolerant to brown streak disease. Uproot and destroy any plants that show the symptoms, and do not take cuttings from those affected areas. This stops the spread by infected cuttings and whitefly. To be sure of the disease and the right tolerant variety, go to ITRA for confirmation.
I see yellow patches along the veins of my cassava leaves and the roots look brown and corky when I pull them up. What is happening?

Use cuttings only from healthy plants and choose a tolerant variety. Then uproot and destroy any plants that show these leaf or root symptoms, and do not take cuttings from those areas. Go to ITRA to have the disease confirmed, because the brown-streak symptoms on roots need checking.
I see yellow blotches along the leaf veins of my cassava plants.
Do you also notice a brown, corky rot inside the roots when you pull a plant up?
Yes, the roots are brown and corky when I dig them up.

Your cassava has cassava brown streak disease. Use cuttings only from healthy plants and choose a tolerant variety for new planting. Uproot and destroy all plants that show the yellow leaf blotches or the brown corky rot in the roots. Do not take any cuttings from the affected area because they can spread the disease. To confirm the diagnosis, take a sample to ITRA for testing.
My goats are showing fever and a muco-purulent discharge from their nose and eyes. What should I do?

This is PPR. Isolate every sick animal right away and stop all movement in and out of the herd. Do not sell or slaughter any animals during the outbreak and dispose of any carcasses safely. Give the sick animals clean water and soft feed to support them. On veterinary advice, vaccinate all healthy and in-contact animals with PPR vaccine. Notify the veterinary service immediately.
I see sores inside the mouths of some of my sheep and they are coughing a lot. Can they recover?

These signs indicate PPR. Isolate every sick animal at once and stop all movement in and out of the herd. Do not sell or slaughter any animals while the disease is present and dispose of any dead animals safely. Provide the sick animals with water and soft feed to keep them nourished. Vaccinate the healthy and in-contact animals with PPR vaccine after consulting a veterinarian. Notify the veterinary service immediately.
My herd has sudden diarrhoea and many goats are dying quickly, almost all of them. What is happening?

This is typical of PPR. Isolate every sick animal at once and stop all movement in and out of the herd. Do not sell or slaughter any animals during the outbreak and dispose of carcasses safely. Give the sick animals water and soft feed to help them. On veterinary advice, vaccinate all healthy and in-contact animals with PPR vaccine. Notify the veterinary service immediately.
How do I manage an outbreak of peste des petits ruminants in my goats?

The disease is PPR. First, isolate every sick animal at once and stop all movement in and out of the herd. Then, do not sell or slaughter any animals while the outbreak lasts and dispose of any carcasses safely. Support the sick animals with water and soft feed. Vaccinate the healthy and in-contact animals with PPR vaccine on veterinary advice. Notify the veterinary service immediately.
goats sudden fever and nose discharge

Your goats are showing classic signs of peste des petits ruminants. Isolate every sick animal right away and stop any movement of animals in and out of the herd. Give the sick animals clean water and soft feed to keep them nourished. Do not sell or slaughter any animals while the outbreak is happening, and make sure any dead animals are disposed of safely. Arrange vaccination for all healthy and in-contact animals as soon as possible, following veterinary advice. Notify the veterinary service immediately for official help.
It looks like contagious caprine pleuropneumonia, so I will just treat with antibiotics

It is not contagious caprine pleuropneumonia, it is peste des petits ruminants. The two are told apart by the signs: PPR gives fever, muco-purulent discharge from nose and eyes, mouth sores, diarrhoea, coughing and rapid deaths, while pleuropneumonia shows different lung signs and needs lab confirmation. Because it is PPR, you must isolate every sick animal at once and stop all movement in and out of the herd. Provide water and soft feed, do not sell or slaughter, and safely dispose of any carcasses. Then vaccinate all healthy and in-contact animals on veterinary advice. Notify the veterinary service immediately.
When exactly should I vaccinate after the outbreak starts?

You should vaccinate all healthy and in-contact animals as soon as possible after you have isolated the sick ones and stopped movement, giving them water and soft feed meanwhile. The vaccine is given on veterinary advice and should follow the isolation and movement stop steps. I cannot give you an exact date for vaccination because that depends on the situation and the veterinary service. Notify the veterinary service immediately; they will tell you the precise timing and provide the vaccine.
My goats have been getting sick and some have died quickly.
Do the sick animals have fever, a muco-purulent discharge from the nose or eyes, and sores inside the mouth?
Yes, they have fever, runny nose and eyes, and sores in their mouths.
